title: AI, next-gen tech, and maritime decarbonization on RINA- China Merchants Energy Shipping pact’s agenda
summary: China Merchants Energy Shipping (CMES), managing over 380 vessels with a staggering 55 million DWT, has signed a non-committal MoU with RINA to "explore" decarbonization and carbon emissions management. This "strategic cooperation" primarily outlines studying AI, alternative fuels, and smart shipping, conspicuously lacking any concrete commitments to actual carbon intensity reductions or immediate HFO phase-out. While CMES and RINA discuss future tech, this massive fleet's current carbon footprint and strategy for avoiding impending FuelEU Maritime fines remain unaddressed.
content:
China Merchants Energy Shipping and RINA’s newly signed memorandum of understanding (MoU) establishes a framework for strategic cooperation across maritime safety, digitalization, operational excellence, and emerging shipping technologies.

This agreement creates a platform for long-term collaboration, enabling the two organizations to combine their expertise and explore opportunities that support innovation and the evolving needs of the maritime sector, expanding on the duo’s existing relationship.

The MoU enables CMES and RINA to look into initiatives related to fleet safety and risk management, carbon emissions management and regulatory compliance, digitalization and data-driven vessel operations, as well as the application of artificial intelligence to areas such as predictive maintenance, energy efficiency and operational decision-making.

The agreement also entails the study of alternative fuels, alongside smart shipping technologies, automation, and other innovations relevant to the future development of the maritime industry.

In addition, it will promote technical exchange, research activities, and knowledge sharing, with the aim of supporting operational excellence and helping both organizations navigate a rapidly evolving regulatory and technological landscape.

CMES Shipping operates and manages more than 380 vessels, with a total deadweight tonnage exceeding 55 million tons, ranking among the top in the world in terms of fleet capacity.
